column1: # Unix group membership and what it is worth to an attacker, matched by the groups detector
# against `id` output. Most groups are harmless; the ones below carry a severity because they
# are, directly or nearly, a path to root or to sensitive data.
# severity  OK | INFO | NOTICE | WARN | CRITICAL
# exploit   a concrete next step the learner can try (kept short; '-' when none)

column3: description
Membership of the root group grants group-owner access to root-group files and is a stepping stone to full root.
column4: hunt for group root-writable binaries and config

column3: Can invoke sudo (Debian/Ubuntu). What you may run as root is the real story.
Can invoke sudo (Arch/Fedora/RHEL) once configured.
Legacy sudo-capable admin group.
The docker group is root: you control the daemon, which runs as root.
The lxd group is root: launch a privileged container with the host disk mounted.
Can create privileged containers with host filesystem access.
column4: same technique as the lxd group

column3: Raw access to block devices - read or write the filesystem directly, bypassing permissions.
Read /etc/shadow directly and crack every password hash offline.
Access to kernel memory via /dev/mem or /dev/kmem.
Read most of /var/log - excellent recon (credentials in logs, command history).
Framebuffer access - screenshot the physical console.
Read input devices - build a keylogger from /dev/input/event*.
Access /dev/kvm and run VMs; occasionally reaches host resources.
Manage libvirt VMs - often equal to root via a VM that mounts the host disk.

Reconfigure network interfaces.
Read the systemd journal - logs and sometimes secrets logged by services.
Write to other users' terminals.
Serial-port access - relevant on IoT/OT hosts.
Manage removable/pluggable devices. Normal for a desktop user.
Generic primary users group. Normal.
